title: Law as command: Austin's sovereign
subtitle: The command theory of law and the cracks in it
objectives: State Austin's command theory precisely: law as the general commands of a sovereign, backed by sanctions, habitually obeyed by the bulk of a political society
Explain Austin's separation thesis — that the existence of law and its moral merit are two distinct enquiries — and place it as the founding move of legal positivism
Identify and explain the three classic objections to command theory: the problem of continuing law, the existence of power-conferring rules, and a sovereign who is himself legally unbound

leadingAuthorities.citation: Austin, The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832), esp. Lecture I and Lecture V
leadingAuthorities.role: The founding text of command theory: defines law as the sovereign's general commands backed by sanctions, and states the separation thesis

leadingAuthorities.citation: Bentham, Of Laws in General (composed 1780s, publ. 1945)
leadingAuthorities.role: Austin's utilitarian predecessor, whose unpublished analysis of law as an expression of sovereign will Austin systematised and popularised

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hart, The Concept of Law (1961), chs 2–4
leadingAuthorities.role: The canonical critique of command theory — previewed at the end of this lesson, developed in full in Lesson 5

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Command theory is the version of positivism examiners expect you to be able to state cleanly and then dismantle — it's the theory this module uses to teach the skill of building an argument before you're shown how it falls. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of understanding, this brief note appears: 'You can define command theory — this lesson is about showing why each of its three pillars is a problem, not just naming them.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on stating the theory before. The test pool below leans towards scenarios: expect 'does this example fit Austin's model' rather than 'define the model'.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and hold the three elements — command, sanction, habitual obedience — firmly before moving on; the whole lesson is built on being able to name them without hesitation.

overview.hook: Imagine a gunman says to a bank clerk, 'Hand over the money or I'll shoot.' The clerk has a reason to comply, and in a sense is obliged to — but most people's instinct is that the clerk isn't under a legal duty and the gunman hasn't made law. John Austin thought the difference between the gunman and a legitimate lawmaker was smaller, and more structural, than you'd expect: repeat the threat, make it general, make people habitually obey it, and remove anyone the threatener himself has to obey — and you have, on Austin's account, exactly what law is. This lesson tests whether that account holds.
overview.lawStatedNotice: This lesson teaches a fixed historical text (1832) and the settled scholarly critique of it. There is no legislative development to track; law stated as at 23 September 2026 reflects only that this content remains current teaching, not that anything has changed.

parts.heading: The gunman writ large
parts.voice: narrative — builds the theory through the gunman analogy before naming its elements
body: John Austin, writing in the 1830s, wanted a science of law stripped of theology and moral argument — a description of what law actually is, as a matter of observable social fact, rather than what it ought to be. His answer: law is a species of command.

A command, for Austin, is an expressed wish that someone do or not do something, backed by the threat of an 'evil' (a sanction) if they disobey. That much fits the gunman perfectly. What turns a mere threat into positive law, on Austin's account, is three further conditions: the command must be general (addressed to a class of acts or persons, not a one-off instruction), it must come from a sovereign, and it must be habitually obeyed by the bulk of the political society in question.

The sovereign is doing most of the work in that definition, and Austin defines the role precisely: a sovereign is a determinate person or body that the bulk of society habitually obeys, and who is not themselves in the habit of obedience to any other determinate human superior. Remove the gunman's threat being one-off and personal, generalise it, route it through an habitually-obeyed sovereign who answers to no one — and you have, on this account, exactly what a legal system is.

components.definition: Austin's account of law: the general commands of a sovereign — a determinate person or body habitually obeyed by the bulk of a political society and not itself habitually obedient to any other human superior — backed by the threat of a sanction for disobedience.

interaction.prompt: On Austin's account, what turns the gunman's one-off threat into something structurally different from law?
options: Generality, a sovereign source, and habitual obedience by the society at large
Nothing — Austin thought the gunman's threat already counted as law
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Austin's gunman analogy is meant to show how close law sits to naked coercion — what separates them, on his account, is structural (generality, sovereignty, habitual obedience), not a difference in kind of force.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — Austin didn't think the gunman himself made law. He used the comparison precisely to isolate what's missing: generality, a sovereign source, and habitual obedience by the wider society, not just a single victim's compliance.

parts.heading: Anatomy of a command: the three working parts
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Break Austin's definition into its components and each does specific analytical work, and each is where a later critic will eventually apply pressure.

Command: an expressed wish, general in scope, that a class of persons do or forbear from some class of acts. Sanction: the 'evil' — punishment, in the ordinary case — threatened for disobedience; Austin thought that without some sanction, however remote or improbable, a rule isn't really a command at all, only advice or an entreaty. Habitual obedience: not perfect, universal compliance, but a general pattern of compliance by the bulk of society, most of the time, over time — enough that the sovereign's authority is a settled social fact rather than a one-off event.

Notice what this account does not require: it does not require the command to be just, wise, or morally defensible. That omission is deliberate, and it's the separation thesis this lesson comes to next.

components.label: The three working parts of a command
points: Command — a general expressed wish that a class of persons do or forbear from some class of acts
Sanction — the threatened 'evil' for disobedience; without one, Austin held, a rule is mere advice
Habitual obedience — sustained, general compliance by the bulk of the political society, not universal or perfect compliance
The sovereign issuing the command must not itself be in the habit of obeying any other determinate human superior

interaction.prompt: Put these in the order Austin's definition builds up a rule into positive law.
items: A determinate sovereign expresses a general wish
The wish is backed by the threat of a sanction for disobedience
The bulk of the political society habitually obeys the wish
The rule counts as positive law, regardless of its moral content
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure: source, sanction, and habitual obedience are all doing separate jobs, and only once all three are in place does Austin call the result law — with moral content deliberately left out of the test.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the sovereign's wish comes first, the sanction is what converts a wish into a command, habitual obedience is what makes the sovereign's authority a social fact, and only then does Austin call the result law.

parts.heading: Why 'is' and 'ought' must stay apart
parts.voice: statute-first — works from Austin's own words outward
body: Austin's most quoted sentence states the separation thesis as bluntly as any positivist ever has: 'The existence of law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another. Whether it be or be not is one enquiry; whether it be or be not conformable to an assumed standard, is a different enquiry.'

This is the founding move of legal positivism as a tradition, and it is worth being precise about what it does and doesn't claim. Austin is not saying morally bad laws are good, or that we shouldn't criticise them — he thought a sufficiently unjust law might be one you have every moral reason to disobey, even resist. What he is saying is that its being unjust has no bearing on whether it is law. Validity is a question of pedigree — did a sovereign command it, is it backed by a sanction, is it habitually obeyed — not a question of moral content.

This directly answers classical natural law's claim, met earlier in this module, that an unjust 'law' is not really law at all (lex injusta non est lex). Austin thinks that slogan confuses two different questions and, by doing so, actually weakens the case against bad laws — because if an evil statute is simply not law, there's nothing to disobey in the first place; on Austin's view, it is law, and identifying it clearly as such is the first step to opposing it as law.

components.citation: Austin, The Province of Jurisprudence Determined, Lecture V
components.text: The existence of law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another. Whether it be or be not is one enquiry; whether it be or be not conformable to an assumed standard, is a different enquiry. A law, which actually exists, is a law, though we happen to dislike it, or though it vary from the text, by which we regulate our approbation and disapprobation.
elements: Validity turns on pedigree (sovereign command, sanction, habitual obedience), not moral content
A law can be law and be bad — the two questions are logically independent
This is a direct rejection of the natural law claim that an unjust rule is not truly law

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Austin's separation thesis claims unjust laws should never be disobeyed or resisted?
sliderLabels: Confident — that is not his claim at all
interaction.correctPosition: that is not his claim at all
interaction.explanation: Austin's claim is narrower and more precise than that. He separates the question 'is it law' from the question 'is it good law' — he does not say bad laws must be obeyed, only that their badness doesn't stop them being law. Whether to resist a bad law is, for Austin, exactly the separate moral enquiry his thesis insists on keeping distinct.

parts.heading: Two rules Austin's model can't easily explain
parts.voice: argumentative — sets up the objections that Lesson 5 will develop in full
body: Two problems surface as soon as you try to run real legal rules through Austin's machine, and both will resurface, sharpened, when Hart's critique arrives in the next lesson.

The first is the problem of continuing law. A statute passed under one monarch remains law after that monarch dies, without being re-commanded by the successor. But a command, on Austin's own account, is a particular act of will by a particular person at a particular time — so how can a command from a dead sovereign still bind? Austin's answer — that the new sovereign tacitly commands the old rules to continue by not repealing them — starts to look strained: silence is being treated as an act of will, which is doing a great deal of theoretical work for very little evidence.

The second is the existence of power-conferring rules — rules that let you make a valid will, form a company, or get married, rather than ordering you to do or not do something. If you get the formalities of a will wrong, the 'sanction' is that the will is void — it simply has no legal effect. But nullity isn't an 'evil' threatened for disobedience in anything like the sense a criminal sanction is; nobody is punished for writing an invalid will, they just fail to achieve what they were trying to achieve. Forcing these facilitative, power-conferring rules into the shape of orders-backed-by-threats distorts what they actually do.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say nullity 'is' a sanction, on the basis that it's clearly an unwelcome consequence of getting the rule wrong.
components.whyItsWrong: Austin's sanction has to be the threatened evil for disobeying a command to do or not do something. A power-conferring rule doesn't command you to make a will at all — it offers you a facility for achieving a legal effect, and nullity is simply the absence of that effect if you don't use the facility correctly. Treating nullity as a 'sanction' collapses a distinction — between rules that order and rules that empower — that later critics (Hart, especially) treat as central to what a mature legal system actually looks like.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that shows the rule in question is power-conferring, not command-and-sanction in Austin's sense.
interaction.scenarioText: Priya signs a document intending it to be her will, but fails to have it witnessed as the Wills Act requires. No one prosecutes her, fines her, or imprisons her for the mistake. The document simply has no legal effect as a will, and her estate passes under the intestacy rules instead.
tappableSpans: signs a document intending it to be her will
No one prosecutes her, fines her, or imprisons her
the document simply has no legal effect
interaction.correctSpan: the document simply has no legal effect
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the tell. Nothing is threatened or inflicted on Priya — she simply fails to achieve the legal effect she was aiming for. That's the signature of a power-conferring rule, which sits awkwardly inside a theory built entirely around commands and sanctions.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the absence of any threatened evil, not the fact of the mistake itself. The tell that this is a power-conferring rule, not a command backed by a sanction, is that Priya isn't punished at all — the rule simply withholds the legal effect she was trying to bring about.

parts.heading: A sovereign bound by no one?
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the problem before naming the difficulty
body: Here's a question worth sitting with before reading on: in the UK today, who is Austin's sovereign — the single determinate person or body, habitually obeyed, who is not in the habit of obeying anyone else?

Parliament looks like the obvious candidate, given the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty you'll meet in Public law. But Parliament itself only counts as Parliament, and only legislates validly, by following rules about how it is constituted and how it must act — rules on royal assent, on what counts as a Bill properly passed, on the very definition of 'the Queen (or King)-in-Parliament'. Those constitutive rules are not themselves commands issued by Parliament, because Parliament could not exist as a lawmaking body without them already being in place. Something logically prior to the sovereign's commands is doing the work of making the sovereign a sovereign at all.

This is the third classic problem: Austin's sovereign is supposed to be legally illimitable, bound by no other human superior — a good fit for an absolute monarch, a poor fit for a modern constitutional state where the lawmaker's own powers are themselves constituted, and often constrained, by rules that don't look like anyone's command. Keep this question open rather than answered: Hart's rule of recognition, which is where Lesson 5 begins, is built almost entirely as a response to it.

components.term: The problem of the illimitable sovereign
components.definition: The objection that Austin's model requires a sovereign not habitually obedient to any other human superior, which fits an absolute monarch but sits awkwardly with a modern state where the lawmaking body's own existence and powers are constituted by rules that precede and are not reducible to that body's own commands.

interaction.prompt: Which of these two lawmaking systems is the closer fit for Austin's model of an illimitable, habitually-obeyed sovereign?
interaction.scenarioA: An absolute monarch whose word, once uttered as a general edict, is treated by officials and subjects alike as binding, with no procedural formalities and no body the monarch must answer to.
interaction.scenarioB: A legislature that can only make valid law by following a detailed constitutive procedure — first reading, committee, royal assent — set out in rules that the legislature itself did not create and cannot simply command away.
interaction.explanation: A is the closer fit: a single, habitually-obeyed will not itself constituted or constrained by prior rules is exactly Austin's model. B is the harder case for command theory — a lawmaker whose very existence and powers depend on constitutive rules that look nothing like commands from a sovereign, which is precisely the gap Hart's account is built to fill.

testPool.prompt: State Austin's definition of positive law in one sentence.
acceptableAnswers: the general commands of a sovereign, backed by sanctions, habitually obeyed
commands backed by threats from a habitually obeyed sovereign
testPool.modelAnswer: Positive law is the general command of a sovereign — a determinate person or body habitually obeyed by the bulk of a political society and not itself habitually obedient to any other human superior — backed by the threat of a sanction for disobedience.

testPool.prompt: Name the three conditions Austin's sovereign must meet for their commands to count as positive law.
acceptableAnswers: generality, sanction, habitual obedience by the society
the command is general, backed by a sanction, and habitually obeyed
testPool.modelAnswer: The command must be general (not a one-off order), backed by the threat of a sanction, and habitually obeyed by the bulk of the political society, with the sovereign itself not habitually obedient to any other determinate human superior.

testPool.prompt: According to Austin, does the moral merit of a rule affect whether it counts as valid law?
options: No — validity turns on pedigree (sovereign command, sanction, habitual obedience), not moral content
Yes — an immoral rule can never be valid law on Austin's account

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of Austin's three elements of a command that counts as positive law?
options: A general expressed wish
A sanction threatened for disobedience
Moral justification for the command's content
Habitual obedience by the bulk of society
testPool.trapExplanation: This is the whole point of the separation thesis: Austin's definition contains no requirement that the command be morally justified. Including 'moral justification' would collapse command theory back into the natural law position Austin is deliberately rejecting.

testPool.prompt: A student argues that a rule allowing valid marriage by following certain formalities is 'really' backed by a sanction, because a couple who get the formalities wrong don't get a valid marriage — and a lack of legal recognition is bad for them. What is the strongest response to this argument?
options: The student is right — any unwelcome consequence of non-compliance counts as an Austinian sanction

Nullity of a facilitative act is not a threatened 'evil' for disobeying an order; the rule offers a facility rather than commanding conduct, and failing to use it correctly is not punished, it simply achieves nothing
Marriage law has no sanction at all and so falls outside Austin's theory entirely, with nothing further to say
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting move is to stretch 'sanction' to cover any unwelcome outcome, but that stretches Austin's own definition past breaking point — a sanction has to be the threatened evil for disobeying a command to act, not the mere absence of a legal effect someone failed to bring about. The precise distinction between commanding and empowering is the objection's whole force.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps of the continuing-law objection to Austin in the correct logical order.
items: A command is defined by Austin as a particular act of will by a particular person at a particular time
A statute passed under one monarch remains law after that monarch dies, without being re-issued
Austin must explain this by treating the new sovereign's silence (non-repeal) as a tacit act of command
Treating silence as an act of will strains the theory's own definition of a command

testPool.prompt: In Austin's own definition — 'a command...obliges a person...to a course of conduct...enforced by a sanction' — which word is doing the theoretical work of distinguishing law from mere advice?
options: 'Sanction' — without a threatened evil for disobedience, Austin held a rule is only advice or entreaty
'Person' — because only orders addressed to a named individual count as law
'Conduct' — because only rules about physical acts, not omissions, count as commands

testPool.prompt: Apply Austin's own text — 'The existence of law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another' — to this claim: 'The Nuremberg Laws could not have been valid German law because they were profoundly unjust.' What would Austin say about this claim?
options: Austin would reject it: injustice bears on whether a law should be obeyed or resisted, not on whether it was, as a matter of fact, law
Austin would accept it without qualification, since he thought unjust rules were automatically invalid
Austin's theory has nothing to say about this question at all
testPool.explanation: This is the separation thesis applied directly: for Austin, whether the Nuremberg Laws were commanded by the sovereign and habitually obeyed is one enquiry (an 'is' question); whether they were just is a separate enquiry entirely. Their injustice is a reason to condemn and resist them, not a reason to deny they were law.

testPool.prompt: In the extract below from Austin, highlight the sentence that most directly states the separation thesis.
testPool.passage: A law, which actually exists, is a law, though we happen to dislike it, or though it vary from the text, by which we regulate our approbation and disapprobation. This truth, when formally announced as an abstract proposition, is so simple and glaring that it seems idle to insist upon it. But simple and glaring as it is, when enunciated in abstract expressions the enumeration of the instances in which it has been forgotten would fill a volume.
testPool.ratioSentence: A law, which actually exists, is a law, though we happen to dislike it, or though it vary from the text, by which we regulate our approbation and disapprobation.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that identifies the problem case for Austin's theory in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: A modern constitutional legislature wants to pass a new statute. Before it can do so validly, it must follow a fixed procedure of readings and royal assent laid down in rules the legislature itself did not create in this Parliament and cannot simply command away by majority vote alone.
tappableSpans: A modern constitutional legislature wants to pass a new statute
it must follow a fixed procedure of readings and royal assent
rules the legislature itself did not create in this Parliament
cannot simply command away by majority vote alone
testPool.correctSpan: rules the legislature itself did not create in this Parliament
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the crux of the illimitable-sovereign problem: rules constituting and constraining the lawmaker precede and are not reducible to that lawmaker's own commands, which Austin's model of a sovereign obedient to no one struggles to accommodate.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact showing the legislature's own power is itself rule-constituted, rather than simply the legislature acting. The problem for Austin is that these constitutive rules exist prior to, and independently of, anything the sovereign has commanded.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario best illustrates the power-conferring rule objection to command theory, rather than the continuing-law objection?
testPool.scenarioA: A criminal statute passed fifty years ago under a different monarch is still enforced today, without ever having been re-enacted or re-commanded by the current sovereign.
testPool.scenarioB: A couple who fail to give the correct notice period before their wedding find that the ceremony, though it took place, does not produce a legally valid marriage — and nobody is punished for the mistake.
testPool.explanation: B is the power-conferring rule problem: the 'consequence' of getting it wrong is nullity, not a sanction in Austin's sense, because the rule was never commanding the couple to marry in the first place — it was offering them a facility. A is the continuing-law problem: a command persisting without being reissued by the current sovereign.

testPool.prompt: A theorist claims a modern constitutional monarch, whose acts require ministerial countersignature and who cannot legally veto legislation passed by the elected chambers, still counts as Austin's 'sovereign'. Applying Austin's own definition, is this claim sound?
options: No — Austin's sovereign must not be habitually obedient to any other determinate human superior, and a monarch legally constrained by ministers and an elected legislature does not fit that description
Yes — anyone bearing the formal title 'sovereign' automatically satisfies Austin's definition
Yes, provided the monarch is habitually obeyed by at least some of the population
testPool.explanation: Austin's definition is functional, not titular: it requires a determinate person or body not itself habitually obedient to any other human superior. A monarch whose acts are legally constrained by ministers and Parliament fails that test, whatever their ceremonial title — which is exactly why locating 'the sovereign' in a modern constitutional state is so difficult for Austin's model.

testPool.prompt: A first-year student writes: 'Austin's theory works fine for criminal law, but the rules that let people make contracts, wills and companies aren't commands at all — so either those rules aren't really law, or Austin's theory is incomplete.' Analyse this claim using Austin's own definition of a command.
factsToOrder: Austin defines law as general commands backed by sanctions and habitually obeyed
Rules enabling wills, contracts and companies confer powers rather than ordering conduct
Non-compliance with a power-conferring rule produces nullity, not a punitive sanction
These rules are uncontroversially treated as part of the legal system by lawyers and courts alike

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether power-conferring rules (for wills, contracts, companies) can be accommodated within Austin's command theory, or expose a genuine gap in it.
modelAnswer.rule: Austin defines law as general commands, backed by sanctions, issued by a sovereign and habitually obeyed. A sanction is the threatened evil for disobeying an order to act; nullity of an act that fails to satisfy formal requirements is not the same kind of consequence.
modelAnswer.application: Power-conferring rules do not order anyone to make a will, contract or company — they offer a facility for achieving a legal effect. Failing to use the facility correctly produces nullity, not punishment: nothing is threatened or inflicted, the intended legal effect simply doesn't arise. Forcing these rules into the command-and-sanction mould, by stretching 'sanction' to include nullity, distorts what the rules actually do, since lawyers plainly treat them as law without treating them as orders.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The student's instinct is broadly right: power-conferring rules are uncontroversially law, but do not fit comfortably inside Austin's command-and-sanction model — this is a genuine limitation of the theory, not a reason to deny these rules are law at all.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that Austin's command theory can straightforwardly explain why a statute remains binding law after the monarch who signed it into being has died?
sliderLabels: Not confident — this is one of the theory's real weak points
testPool.correctPosition: Not confident — this is one of the theory's real weak points
testPool.explanation: This is the continuing-law problem. Austin's own definition treats a command as a particular act of will by a particular person at a particular time, so explaining why a rule persists without being re-commanded requires treating the new sovereign's silence as a tacit command — a move most later commentators, including Hart, treat as a genuine strain on the theory rather than a clean solution.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating any unwelcome consequence of breaking a rule as an Austinian 'sanction'. It isn't — a sanction is the threatened evil for disobeying a command to act, and power-conferring rules (wills, contracts, marriage) don't command anything at all, which is exactly why they're the theory's hardest case.
